Problem 3. Stewart-Tolman Effect

In 1917, Stewart and Tolman discovered a flow of current through a coil wound around a cylinder rotated axially with certain angular acceleration.

Consider a great number of rings, with the radius $\tau$ each, made of a thin metallic wire with resistance $R$. The rings have been put in a uniform way on very long glass cylinder, which is vacuum inside. Their positions on the cylinder are fixed by gluing the rings to the cylinder. The number of rings per unit of length along the symmetry axis is $n$. The planes containing the rings are perpendicular to the symmetry axis of the cylinder.

At some moment the cylinder starts a rotational movement around its symmetry axis with an acceleration $\alpha$. Find the value of the magnetic field $B$ at the center of the cylinder (after a sufficiently long time). We assume that the electric charge $e$ of an electron, and the electron mass $m$ are known.

Question 7

[Set-up of Question 6: Ali and Beatrice are doing an experiment to measure the spring constant, $k$, of a spring. Ali uses a static method, using the equation $k=\frac{F_{\text{applied}}}{s}=\frac{mg}{s}$, where $m$ is the mass of a weight attached to the hanging spring, and $s$ is the distance that the spring stretches by.]

Ali has spent too much time deciding what to do, and only takes one pair of measurements. He measures the mass of the weight to be $(100\pm5)\,\mathrm{g}$ and the stretch, $s$, when he hangs it on the spring to be $(5.0\pm0.5)\,\mathrm{cm}$. Based on these data, the spring constant is:

a. $(20.0\pm0.2)\,\mathrm{N/m}$

b. $(20\pm3)\,\mathrm{N/m}$

c. $(20\pm6)\,\mathrm{N/m}$

d. $(200\pm20)\,\mathrm{N/m}$

e. $(200\pm30)\,\mathrm{N/m}$

Question 2

Which of the following is the best estimate of the speed of a parrot flying?

a. $3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

b. $1\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

c. $3\times10^{0}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

d. $1\times10^{2}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

e. $3\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

Question 5

Imagine that you are an observer on a planet of a nearby star such as Proximae Centauri (if it has one). You might notice that our Sun seems to wobble slightly with a somewhat complex wobble. This observed wobble has been used to detect planets round other stars.

i) What is the wobble due to?

ii) Using the data provided find the maximum speed of the wobble.

iii) What other method might be used to detect a planet orbiting a distant star?

[Editorial note: "the data provided" are on the "Important constants" page printed at the front of the paper; the relevant values are:]

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|l|} \hline \text{Mass of the Sun} & M_\mathrm{s} & 2.0\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \hline \text{Distance of Jupiter from the Sun} & R_\text{Jupiter} & 78\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{km} \\ \hline \text{Mass of the Earth} & M_E & 6.0\times10^{24}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \hline \text{Mass of Jupiter} & M_J & 1.9\times10^{27}\,\mathrm{kg} \\ \hline \text{Orbital period of Jupiter} & T_J & 4332\text{ Earth days} \\ \hline \text{Gravitational constant} & G & 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Question 3

Calculate the approximate speed of Nitrogen molecules at a temperature of $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Calculate the height at which the density of the Nitrogen molecules becomes one per cent of the pressure at ground level. It has been suggested that if a plane achieved a suborbital flight to Australia then a great deal of fuel could be saved. Estimate the energy needed to reach a suitable height so that the resistance of the air would be very small.

The "Dreamliner" has a mass of $2.27\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

Problem 3

Deuterium is the heavy stable isotope of hydrogen, having a proton and neutron in its nucleus (protons and neutrons have approximately the same mass). Heavy water is a form of water that contains Deuterium and Oxygen. A heavy water nuclear reactor has heavy water between the nuclear fuel rods. Suppose that a neutron from the fuel rod has a head-on elastic collision with a Dueterium nucleus.

a) Find the ratio of the final speed of the deuteron to the initial speed of the neutron.

b) What percentage of the initial kinetic energy is transferred to the deuteron?

c) How many such collisions is needed to slow down the neutron from 20 MeV to 0.02 eV?

d) How would this estimate change if we consider collisions at other angles?

Question 2

A rocket generates a thrust force by ejecting hot gases from an engine. If it takes $1\,\mathrm{ms}$ to combust $1\,\mathrm{kg}$ of fuel, ejecting it at a speed of $1000\,\mathrm{m/s}$, what thrust is generated?

(a) $1000\,\mathrm{N}$

(b) $10{,}000\,\mathrm{N}$

(c) $100{,}000\,\mathrm{N}$

(d) $1{,}000{,}000\,\mathrm{N}$

Problem 7 [20 points]

1. Suppose that monochromatic light with photon energy $E$ is incident normally on an ideal reflecting mirror (no absorption) of mass $M$ moving with velocity $V$ along the direction of incidence of the light. Using the picture of collisions between photons and the mirror, determine the photon energy $E'$ of the reflected light. The following approximation may be used: $\dfrac{E}{Mc^2}\ll\dfrac{V}{c}\ll1$, where $c$ is the speed of light.

2. If in the problem above the intensity of the monochromatic light is $\Phi$, find the intensity $\Phi'$ of the reflected light (it may be assumed approximately that after the photons strike the mirror, the velocity of the mirror is still $V$). The intensity of light is defined as the energy of the photons passing per unit time through unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the light.

Problem 4: Sinking of a shot

An athletics shot of mass $m = 7.26\,\mathrm{kg}$, made of steel of density $\varrho_\mathrm{k} = 7\,800\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$, is placed below the surface of a deep water reservoir and released.

a) What terminal velocity will the shot reach during its sinking to the bottom?

b) What velocity will the shot gain during the first second of sinking and how deep will it sink in this time?

Solve problem b) by numerical modelling with the Euler method with time step $h = 0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. We assume that the Newton formula $F_\mathrm{o} = \frac{1}{2}CS\varrho v^2$ holds for the drag of the medium. Density of water $\varrho = 1\,000\,\mathrm{kg\cdot m^{-3}}$, drag coefficient $C = 0.48$.

[Editorial note: the paper states for all problems: "In all problems use the gravitational acceleration $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$."]

Problem 1

A cyclist rode a mountain bike without mudguards on a wet horizontal road. At what speed was he moving, if the radius of the tyres is $R$ and the drops splashed from the tyres reached at most a height $h_{\max} > 2R$ above the road? We neglect air resistance.

Solve in general form and for the values $R = 35\,\mathrm{cm}$, $h_{\max} = 2.0\,\mathrm{m}$, $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$.

Superconducting mesh

Consider a mesh made from a flat superconducting sheet by drilling a dense grid of small holes into it. Initially the sheet is in a non-superconducting state, and a magnetic dipole of dipole moment $m$ is at a distance $a$ from the mesh pointing perpendicularly towards the mesh. Now the mesh is cooled so that it becomes superconducting. Next, the dipole is displaced perpendicularly to the surface of the mesh so that its new distance from the mesh is $b$. Find the force between the mesh and the dipole. The pitch of the grid of holes is much smaller than both $a$ and $b$, and the linear size of the sheet is much larger than both $a$ and $b$.

Motion of a charged ball

A solid, homogeneous spherical ball of mass $m$ and radius $R$ is made of insulating material and has charge $Q$ distributed uniformly throughout its volume. The ball is placed on a large horizontal surface, and set in rolling motion without slipping in such a way that its center starts to move with initial horizontal velocity $v_0$. There is a uniform magnetic field (flux density) of magnitude $B$ perpendicular to the surface. The coefficient of static friction is large enough to prevent the ball from slipping on the surface. The moment of inertia of the ball about an axis through its center is $2mR^2/5$.

Describe the motion of the center of the ball and the shape of its trajectory.

Hint: Depending on your approach you may use the following identity:

$$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{b}\,(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}) - \vec{c}\,(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$$

valid for any three vectors $\vec{a}$, $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$.

Problem 3

A. A cylinder contains an ideal gas and is closed at one end by a massless piston of area $S$. The cylinder and the piston are made of thermally insulating material, while inside there is a resistor of resistance $r$, through which an electric current $I$ flows. The piston moves slowly with constant speed $v$. Find the molar specific heat of the gas in this process. The atmospheric pressure is $P$, the Boltzmann constant $K$ and the Avogadro number $N_A$.

B. In the transfer of electrical energy from a DC generator to a consumer located at a distance $d$ from the generator, a copper transmission line is used. The potential difference across the terminals of the generator is $V$ and the power it delivers to the external circuit is $P$. If the maximum permitted power loss in the transmission line is 5% of the power $P$ of the generator, calculate the minimum permitted cross-section of the transmission line. The resistivity of copper is $\rho$.

Problem 3: "Pulling the tablecloth off abruptly"

A cork stopper rests at a distance $\delta = 0.25\,\mathrm{m}$ from one end of a table of length $2\,\mathrm{m}$. The table is covered with a tablecloth whose dimensions are exactly those of the table surface. Suddenly we pull the tablecloth horizontally with acceleration $\alpha = 8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

When the stopper has covered a distance of $0.75\,\mathrm{m}$ it stops resting on the tablecloth and starts sliding on the table. After sliding on the table for another $1\,\mathrm{m}$ it leaves it and falls to the floor at a horizontal distance of $0.8\,\mathrm{m}$ from the point where it left the table.

Also given: $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, the height of the table $h = 0.80\,\mathrm{m}$, and the dimensions of the stopper are negligible. Find the coefficients of friction

(A) between the stopper and the tablecloth

(B) between the stopper and the surface of the table

Consider a circle of radius $R$. A point charge lies at a distance $a$ from its center and on its axis such that $R = a\sqrt{3}$. If electric flux passing through the circle is $\phi$ then the magnitude of the point charge is

(a) $\sqrt{3}\epsilon_0\phi$

(b) $2\epsilon_0\phi$

(c) $4\epsilon_0\phi/\sqrt{3}$

(d) $4\epsilon_0\phi$

An opaque sphere of radius $R$ lies on a horizontal plane. On the perpendicular through the point of contact, there is a point source of light at a distance $R$ above the top of the sphere (i.e. $3R$ from the plane).

(a) [2] Find the area of the shadow of the sphere on the plane.

(b) [6] A transparent liquid of refractive index $\sqrt{3}$ is filled above the plane such that the sphere is just covered with liquid. Find the area of the shadow of the sphere on the plane now.

Experimental part (Mechanics)

There are given two cylindrical bodies (having identical external shapes and from the same material), two measuring rules, one graduated and other un-graduated, and a vessel with water.

It is known that one of the bodies is homogenous and the other has an internal cavity with the following characteristics:

• the cavity is cylindrical
• has the axis parallel with the axis of the body
• its length is practically equal with that of the body

Determine experimentally and justify theoretically:

• a) The density of the material the two bodies consist of.
• b) The radius of the internal cavity.
• c) The distance between the axis of the cavity and the axis of the cylinder.
• d) Indicate the sources of errors and appreciate which of them influences more the final results.

Write all the variants you have found.

Problem 3.

A small charged ball of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is suspended from the highest point of a ring of radius $R$ by means of an insulating cord of negligible mass. The ring is made of a rigid wire of negligible cross section and lies in a vertical plane. On the ring there is uniformly distributed charge $Q$ of the same sign as $q$. Determine the length $l$ of the cord so as the equilibrium position of the ball lies on the symmetry axis perpendicular to the plane of the ring.

Find first the general solution a then for particular values $Q=q=9.0\cdot10^{-8}\,\mathrm{C}$, $R=5\,\mathrm{cm}$, $m=1.0\,\mathrm{g}$, $\varepsilon_0=8.9\cdot10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$.

Problem 3C

Bubbles in carbonated drinks

When a carbonated drink such as soda (サイダー) is uncorked, bubbles can be seen forming near the walls of the container and rising. Observing them carefully, one finds that the bubbles increase their speed as they rise. In contrast, when an air bubble is put into water, it rises at an almost constant velocity. Explain briefly why such a difference occurs.

Problem 3

C

Clouds are collections of minute water droplets floating in the atmosphere. The diameter of these droplets is about $3\sim10\,\mathrm{\mu m}$ ($1\,\mathrm{\mu m}=1\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}$). These droplets are minute, but their density is equal to that of water and much larger than the density of the atmosphere. For this reason, it is puzzling that clouds float in the atmosphere.

Why do clouds not fall down? And what has to happen to the droplets in a cloud for them to fall as rain? Answer the following questions.

Q1. Suppose that an air mass containing a lot of water vapour has formed in the atmosphere near the ground. Describe, in about 120 characters, the process by which this air mass becomes a cloud high up in the sky.

Q2. Why do clouds not fall down? Describe it in about 80 characters.

Q3. Considering the relative motion of the water droplets in the cloud and of the atmosphere containing a lot of water vapour, describe, in about 200 characters, the process until rain begins to fall.

3. Rocket (5 points) — Jaan Kalda.

A photon rocket is accelerated by a laser beam sent from the ground: the rocket's mirror reflects the photons in the exact opposite direction. The rocket's rest mass $M_0$ did not change during the ride. The total energy of the photons emitted by the laser (and later reflected by the rocket) is $\alpha M_0 c^2$. The laser power is constant over time.

i) (1 point) What speed $v$ does the rocket reach if $\alpha = 1 \times 10^{-6}$?

ii) (2 points) What speed $v$ does the rocket reach if $\alpha = 1$?

iii) (2 points) How many times does the rocket's acceleration, as perceived by passengers (i.e. the inertial force acting on them) differ at the beginning and at the end of the acceleration if $\alpha = 1$? Express the answer in terms of the rocket's final speed $v$.

Charges in E (8 points)

Two particles (the blue and the red) of mass $m$ are connected with a spring, the stress-free length of which is $L$ and stiffness $k$; the blue carries charge $q$ ($q > 0$) and the red is chargeless. In the region $x > 0$, there is an homogeneous electric field $E$, antiparallel to the $x$-axis; In the region $x < 0$, there is no electric field. Initially, the “dumbbell” of charges moves in region $x < 0$ with velocity $v$, parallel to the $x$-axis; the dumbbell's axis is also parallel to the $x$-axis and the spring is stress-free. It is known that after a while, the dumbbell moves in the region $x < 0$ with velocity $-v$, and that the red particle never enters the region $x > 0$. Also, the spring's length achieves minimum only once.

i) (2.5 pt) How long time $\tau$ does the blue particle spend in the region $x > 0$?

The process takes place exactly as described, if one equality and one inequality are satisfied for the quantities $m$, $v$, $k$, $q$, $E$ and $L$.

ii) (3 pt) Which equality must be satisfied?

iii) (2.5 pt) Which inequality must be satisfied?

Two small particles, each with a mass of $m = 0.1\ \mathrm{g}$, are at rest in vacuum at a distance $L = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from each other. One particle has a charge $Q = 0.1\ \mathrm{\mu C}$, the other the same charge but opposite. The particles are then released.
Calculate how long it takes for the particles to touch each other. (You do not need to take into account energy loss by bremsstrahlung.) (Hint: Kepler's third law is useful in working out a solution.)

Problem 2: Photoelectric effect for zinc

Light with a net intensity of $1.0\,\mathrm{\mu W/cm^2}$ falls on a clean zinc sample with a surface area of $1.0\,\mathrm{cm^2}$. Zinc reflects 96% of the light, and only 3.0% of the absorbed light lies in the violet part of the spectrum, above the threshold frequency. What is the intensity of the light that is actually available for the photoelectric effect?

(a) If we assume that all photons in the violet region have an effective wavelength of $250\,\mathrm{nm}$ ($1\,\mathrm{nm}=10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m}$), how many electrons are emitted per second? Assume that the photoelectric emission is 100% efficient.
(b) Determine the current in the phototube.
(c) If the cut-off wavelength is $288\,\mathrm{nm}$, determine the work function of zinc.
(d) Determine the stopping voltage if the photoelectrons are produced by light of wavelength $250\,\mathrm{nm}$.

Charlie And The Chocolate Factory

A professional pastry chef is making a sweet which consists of 3 sheets of chocolate. The chef leaves a gap with width $d_1 = 0.1\,\mathrm{m}$ between the top and middle layers and fills it with a chocolate syrup with uniform viscosity $\eta_1 = 10\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$ and a gap with width $d_2 = 0.2\,\mathrm{m}$ between the middle and bottom sheet and fills it with caramel with uniform viscosity $\eta_2 = 15\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$. If the chef pulls the top sheet with a velocity $2\,\mathrm{m/s}$ horizontally, at what speed must he push the bottom sheet horizontally such that the middle sheet remains stationary initially? Ignore the weight of the pastry sheets throughout the problem and the assume the sheets are equally sized.

Note: Shear stress is governed by the equation $\tau = \eta\times\text{rate of strain}$.

Gravitational Oscillations 2

Let the density right at the center of the planet be $\rho_0 = 10000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, and let the height of the disk be $h = 100\,\mathrm{km}$. What is the mass enclosed in the ring with outer radius $R = 6000\,\mathrm{km}$ and inner radius $R - \epsilon$, where $\epsilon = 1\,\mathrm{km}$?

Oscillating octagon

Find all non-trivial natural oscillation frequencies for a regular octagon made from eight homogeneous bars of mass $m$ and length $l$. While the bars are rigid, the connectors connecting two neighboring bars are such that the angle $\varphi$ between the bars can be changed without any friction, but a returning torque $T=k(\varphi-\frac 34\pi)$ will appear at the joint as soon as the angle departs from its equilibrium value $\frac 34\pi$. Indicate how many linearly independent oscillation modes correspond to each of these frequencies. Consider only planar oscillation modes, i.e. modes by which the bars move only in the plane of the octagon.

Bouncing ball

An elastic ball of negligible size is dropped vertically onto a frictionless inclined plane which makes an angle $\alpha$ with the horizontal. Initially the distance between the plane and the ball is $d$ and the speed of the ball is zero. The trajectory of the bouncing ball consists of parabolic arcs. Show that the foci of these parabolic arcs lie on a well-known shape, and give the parameter(s) defining this shape.

Assume that collisions are perfectly elastic and that air drag is negligible.

Death Race pilot

A Death Race pilot traveling at speed $v_0$ suddenly sees a long, high wall across the road ahead. To avoid a collision, the pilot can either

1. [1 point]: Slam on the brakes,

2. [2 points]: Simply swerve (without breaking) to the side (his trajectory will form a circle in this case), or

3. [7 points]: Swerve to the side while simultaneously breaking with the rear wheels. In this case, using steering, the friction force which acts on the rear wheels, can change its direction. The pilot trajectory is still assumed to be circular.

Which of these three methods is more effective (and by how much?), i.e., which method would be preferable to avoid a collision with the nearest obstacle? To estimate this efficiency, calculate, in each case, the distance $L$ (from the wall) between the start of the pilot action and the full stop of the auto. Total mass (pilot + car) is $M$. The coefficient of friction between the wheels of the racer and the road is $\mu$. Assume that the total weight (pilot + car) is equally distributed between front and rear wheels.

End of question.

Elementary particles

The resonance $\Delta^{++}$ (their mass is 1232 $MeV/c^2$) has a full with of $\Gamma = 120\ MeV$.

a) How far on average would such a particle of kinetic energy 200 $GeV$ travel before decaying?

b) This resonance decay following the process: $\Delta^{++} \to X + \pi^+$. Determine the following properties of X: i) electric charge; ii) baryon number, lepton number, isospin, strangeness, it is boson or fermion; iii) lower limit on its mass in $MeV/c^2$; iv) identify this particle.

c) Show the relationship between the pion energy in the laboratory frame ($E_\pi$) and its angle relative to the $\Delta^{++}$ beam ($\theta$), for small angles.

d) In the frame of the quark model draw the diagram of the decay process.

($\hbar c = 197\ MeV\cdot fm$; $c = 3\cdot\frac{10^8m}{s}$, $m_{\pi^+} = 140MeV/c^2$, $m_p = 940MeV/c^2$)

Prof. Ionel Lazanu - University of Bucharest

Problem 3 [20 points]

Three small bodies with different masses $m_1$, $m_2$, $m_3$ are each acted on only by the forces of mutual gravitational attraction. Initially these bodies were at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $b_0$.

a) Prove that a motion of the bodies is possible such that their mutual distances remain unchanged. Determine the angular velocity $\omega_\mathrm{r}$ of rotation of the triangle whose vertices are determined by the positions of the bodies.

b) Prove that a motion of the bodies in the plane determined by their initial positions is possible such that their mutual distances change but remain equal to one another (the triangle whose vertices are determined by the positions of the bodies is always equilateral).

c) At the initial instant the velocities of the bodies are such as if the triangle were rotating without change of size, in its own plane, with angular velocity $\omega_0$ smaller than the angular velocity $\omega_\mathrm{r}$ from part a). Calculate the minimum length of the side of the triangle $b_\mathrm{min}$ that will occur during the motion of the bodies.

Problem 2 [20 points]

A closed circular circuit (a loop) is located in a uniform magnetic field of varying induction. In the time interval $0 < t < t_0$ this induction is given by the formula

$$B(t) = B_0\left(1 - \left(\frac{t}{t_0}\right)^2\right),$$

where $B_0$ and $t_0$ are constant parameters. The loop has radius $r$ and is made of wire with resistance per unit length $\rho$. The plane of the circuit is perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

Determine the minimum breaking strength $W$ of the wire such that the loop does not break in the time interval $0 < t < t_0$.

Give the numerical value of this strength for $B_0 = 4\ \mathrm{T}$, $t_0 = 0.2\ \mathrm{s}$, $r = 10\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\rho = 0.1\ \Omega/\mathrm{m}$.

Neglect the extensibility (elasticity) of the wire and assume that the induction of the magnetic field due to the current flowing in the loop is much smaller than the induction of the external field.

The breaking strength of a wire is the maximum force stretching it at which it does not break.

Problem 2: Exploring a planet

A descent module is landing on the surface of an exotic planet. During the descent the dependence of the pressure $p$ in the atmosphere of the planet on the distance $z$ to the surface of the planet was measured (graph on a separate sheet). A temperature measurement made at the height $z_1 = 5~\mathrm{km}$ gave the value $T_1 = 250~\mathrm{K}$. Calculate the temperature $T_0$ at the surface of the planet. Assume that the radius of the planet $R \gg z_1$. The atmosphere consists of carbon dioxide.

Note. The graph on the separate sheet must be handed in together with your solution.

[Editorial note: the graph on the separate sheet is not included in the official task file.]

Problem 4: Space object

A space object moving along a certain straight line with constant velocity emits periodic radio pulses. An astronomer established that during the observation time $\Delta t$ the apparent direction to this object changed by a small angle $\Delta\varphi$, and the period between the moments of arrival of the radio pulses changed from $T$ to $T + \Delta T$, where $\Delta T \ll T$. Find the distance from the observer to the object. The speed of the radio pulses is equal to the speed of light $c$.

Problem 2: Danger zone

As is well known, crows are very clever birds that sensitively recognise imminent danger and know how to avoid it. On a horizontal field, above which crows fly, stands a boy who shoots small pebbles at the crows from a slingshot.

a) Determine the smallest distance from the boy at which the crows can walk about on the field and be safe from being hit by pebbles from the slingshot.

b) Determine the smallest horizontal distance from the boy, as a function of the height $h$ above the ground, at which the crows can fly and the boy still cannot hit them.

c) Determine the radius of the circle into which crows flying at the height $h=25\,\mathrm{m}$ should not fly in order not to be in danger of being hit by a pebble from the slingshot, if the boy shoots the pebbles at the speed $v_0=40\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-1}}$.

Neglect air resistance and the height of the boy; the gravitational acceleration is $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m\cdot s^{-2}}$.

Question A2

A solid round object of radius $R$ can roll down an incline that makes an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal. Assume that the rotational inertia about an axis through the center of mass is given by $I = \beta mR^2$. The coefficient of kinetic and static friction between the object and the incline is $\mu$. The object moves from rest through a vertical distance $h$.

a. If the angle of the incline is sufficiently large, then the object will slip and roll; if the angle of the incline is sufficiently small, then the object with roll without slipping. Determine the angle $\theta_c$ that separates the two types of motion.

b. Derive expressions for the linear acceleration of the object down the ramp in the case of

i. Rolling without slipping, and

ii. Rolling and slipping.

Question A3

A light bulb has a solid cylindrical filament of length $L$ and radius $a$, and consumes power $P$. You are to design a new light bulb, using a cylindrical filament of the same material, operating at the same voltage, and emitting the same spectrum of light, which will consume power $nP$. What are the length and radius of the new filament? Assume that the temperature of the filament is approximately uniform across its cross-section; the filament doesn’t emit light from the ends; and energy loss due to convection is minimal.

The table is covered with a tablecloth whose dimensions are exactly those of the table surface. Suddenly we pull the tablecloth horizontally with acceleration $\alpha = 8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

When the stopper has covered a distance of $0.75\,\mathrm{m}$ it stops resting on the tablecloth and starts sliding on the table. After sliding on the table for another $1\,\mathrm{m}$ it leaves it and falls to the floor at a horizontal distance of $0.8\,\mathrm{m}$ from the point where it left the table.

Also given: $g = 10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, the height of the table $h = 0.80\,\mathrm{m}$, and the dimensions of the stopper are negligible. Find the coefficients of friction

(A) between the stopper and the tablecloth

(B) between the stopper and the surface of the table

Problem 5

A thin board of weight w is held vertical at some height above the ground, as it is held between the palms of our hands. If we reduce the pressure between the board and our palms, the board, sliding, acquires an acceleration of magnitude $\alpha=0.1g$, while it receives a normal force $F=\dfrac{3w}{2}$ from each palm.

The coefficient of friction μ between each palm and the surface of the board is equal to:

(i) 0.3 (ii) 0.4 (iii) 0.5 (iv) 0.6

[10 marks]

Problem 3

A farmer lets an object of $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ fall from the window of a barn. A haystack is located $10\,\mathrm{m}$ below the window of the barn. Consider the air resistance negligible and the acceleration due to gravity $g=10\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

(a) Determine the kinetic energy of the object at the instant just before it hits the haystack.

(b) Determine the velocity of the object at the instant just before it hits the haystack.

(c) The object receives a force from the haystack with a mean value of $150\,\mathrm{N}$. How far will the object penetrate into the haystack until it stops?

(d) Determine the magnitude and the direction of the acceleration of the object as it penetrates into the haystack.

(e) Use your answers to the above questions to make the velocity–time graph of the motion of the object from the instant it enters the haystack until the instant it stops.

Problem 2

A. Giannis grows his tomatoes in a small greenhouse. The table shows the change of the temperature during one day, starting from 9 a.m.

(a) Make a graph that shows the change of the temperature with time.

(b) What is the maximum temperature in K?

(c) For how long is the temperature above $36\,^{\mathrm{o}}\mathrm{C}$?

(d) So that the tomatoes would not overheat, Giannis should have opened the door as soon as the temperature exceeded $30\,^{\mathrm{o}}\mathrm{C}$, but he forgot. At what time should he have opened the door?

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Time in h} & \text{Temperature in } ^{\mathrm{o}}\mathrm{C} \\ \hline 0 & 24 \\ 1 & 28 \\ 2 & 32 \\ 3 & 36 \\ 4 & 39 \\ 5 & 40 \\ 6 & 38 \\ 7 & 36 \\ 8 & 33 \end{array}$$

B. The waterfalls of Edessa, unique in Greece, run through and adorn the park of the same name in the centre of the town. At the great waterfall "Karanos" the water falls from a height of 70 metres. Find the maximum possible temperature difference of the water at the top and at the bottom of the waterfall.
